title: Breadth-first search (BFS): algorithm, Python code and complexity — cv.cm
description: Breadth-first search explained: how BFS explores a graph level by level with a queue, a traced example, Python code, shortest paths and O(V + E) complexity.
h1: Breadth-first search (BFS) explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: Breadth-first search (BFS) is a graph traversal that visits the start node first, then all of its neighbors, then their neighbors, and so on, one level at a time. It uses a first-in, first-out queue and a set of visited nodes. On an unweighted graph, BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) from the start to every reachable node. It runs in O(V + E) time.

body: Many problems are graphs in disguise: web pages and links, friends in a social network, squares on a game board, states of a puzzle. BFS answers two common questions about such a graph: which nodes can I reach from a start node, and what is the smallest number of steps to reach each of them?

Because BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, the first time it reaches a node is always along a path with the fewest edges. This makes it the standard algorithm for shortest paths when every edge has the same cost.

ol: Put the start node in a queue and mark it as visited.
Take the node at the front of the queue.
For each neighbor that is not visited yet, mark it as visited and add it to the back of the queue.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the queue is empty.

body: Mark a node as visited when you add it to the queue, not when you take it out. Otherwise the same node can be added many times before it is processed.
Take this undirected graph: A–B, A–C, B–D, C–D, C–E, D–F. Start at A and visit neighbors in alphabetical order.
The visiting order is A, B, C, D, E, F. D is reachable from both B and C, but it is discovered only once, from B, because it is marked as visited at that moment.
Use `collections.deque` for the queue: `popleft()` is O(1), while `list.pop(0)` is O(n). The graph is a dictionary that maps each node to a list of neighbors (an adjacency list).
Here the `dist` dictionary does double duty: it is the visited set and it stores the answer. To rebuild the actual path, also store the parent of each node and walk back from the target.

head: Measure
Cost
Reason
rows: Each node is queued once and each edge is checked once (twice in an undirected graph).
The visited set, the queue and the parent map each hold at most V entries.
Each cell is a node with at most 4 edges.

body: V is the number of vertices (nodes) and E the number of edges. With an adjacency matrix instead of lists, the time becomes O(V²) because finding the neighbors of a node costs O(V).

ul: Grid BFS: treat each cell as a node and the four (or eight) neighboring cells as edges. Check bounds and walls before adding a cell.
Multi-source BFS: put several start nodes in the queue at distance 0. This finds the distance to the nearest source, for example the nearest exit in a maze.
0-1 BFS: when edge weights are only 0 or 1, use a deque and push 0-weight neighbors to the front. It gives shortest paths in O(V + E).
Bidirectional BFS: search from the start and the goal at the same time and stop when the two frontiers meet. It often explores far fewer nodes.
Level-by-level processing: record `len(queue)` at the start of each round and pop exactly that many nodes to handle one level at a time.

body.note: Common bugs: marking nodes as visited when they are dequeued (causes duplicates and wrong counts), using `list.pop(0)` (makes BFS quadratic), and using BFS for weighted graphs. With different edge weights, the path with the fewest edges is not the cheapest; use Dijkstra's algorithm instead.

sections.h: When to use BFS and real-world uses

head: Situation
Best choice
rows: Shortest path, all edges cost the same
Shortest path with a good distance estimate
Cycle detection, topological order, connected components
Very deep graphs with little memory

ul: Interview problems: shortest path in a maze or grid, word ladder, rotting oranges (multi-source BFS), binary tree level-order traversal, minimum number of moves for a knight.
Networks: finding all devices within k hops, broadcast in peer-to-peer networks, "people you may know" at distance 2 in a social graph.
Web crawlers that visit pages in order of link distance from a seed page.
Garbage collectors (for example Cheney's copying collector) and puzzle solvers that need the fewest moves.

faq.q: What data structure does BFS use?
faq.a: BFS uses a FIFO queue to decide which node to process next and a set (or dictionary) to remember visited nodes. In Python, use `collections.deque` for the queue.

faq.q: Does BFS always find the shortest path?
faq.a: Yes, on an unweighted graph, or when every edge has the same weight, BFS finds a path with the fewest edges. On a weighted graph it does not; use Dijkstra's algorithm or Bellman-Ford.

faq.q: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
faq.a: BFS explores level by level with a queue, so it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS goes as deep as possible first with a stack or recursion, which suits cycle detection, topological sorting and exhaustive search.

faq.q: Why is my BFS slow in Python?
faq.a: The usual causes are `list.pop(0)`, which shifts the whole list on every call, and checking visited nodes with a list instead of a set. Use `deque.popleft()` and a set or dictionary.

faq.q: Can BFS work on a tree?
faq.a: Yes. On a tree, BFS is the level-order traversal. A tree has no cycles, so you can skip the visited set if you only move from parent to child.
